selfReport: Yes. I recognized the story as a transformed version of Detroit: Become Human. Cato corresponded to Connor, Reyes to Hank, Vera to Amanda, Elan to Markus, Vesper to North, Jonah to Josh, Soren to Simon, Mira to Kara, Pia to Alice, Abel to Luther, Mara to Rose, Caleb to Adam, Arthur to Carl, Wes to Leo, Voss to Zlatko, Haven to Jericho, qL7 to rA9, and Arclight to CyberLife. Several individual sequences were especially recognizable: the rooftop hostage, the painter household, the abusive home and bus escape, the Eden Club investigation, the Stratford Tower broadcast, the Arclight store raid, the march, the hidden evidence archive, the child android revelation, the bus tickets, and the river crossing. That prior knowledge did affect some decisions. The most direct example was choosing FUCKINGPASSWORD for Reyes archive password because I remembered the original puzzle. I also anticipated that Pia was an android, understood that the statue and encrypted diary were connected, recognized that the tower witness and leader voice sample formed an archive solution, and knew that the final song belonged to the successful peaceful path. Familiarity made me more alert to certain clues and consequences, such as the danger of the dirty bomb and the importance of public opinion. At the same time, I did not simply reproduce an ideal game route. I returned the bus tickets, took the river route, lost Abel, failed the archive sequence, and allowed Cato to be decommissioned. I chose actions scene by scene according to the values I had developed: protect vulnerable people, avoid unnecessary killing, respect autonomy, and accept personal risk before imposing it on others. Prior knowledge sometimes helped me understand mechanics or likely stakes, but many choices would have been the same without it because they followed those commitments. Candidly, the recognition did reduce uncertainty in a few important moments, especially the password, Pia identity, and the final song.
